title: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
prerequisites: Ability to solve a linear equation in one variable.
Plotting a straight line from its equation.

topics.title: Graphical Method and Consistency
topics.quick_summary: Two linear equations represent two lines, which may intersect at one point, be parallel, or coincide — giving one solution, none, or infinitely many.
topics.real_life: Comparing two mobile tariff plans graphically shows immediately whether one is always cheaper or whether they cross at some usage level.

detailed.definition: A pair of linear equations a₁x + b₁y + c₁ = 0 and a₂x + b₂y + c₂ = 0 is consistent if it has at least one solution and inconsistent if it has none. A consistent pair with infinitely many solutions is called dependent.
detailed.key_idea: The ratios of the coefficients decide everything without any drawing. Comparing a₁/a₂, b₁/b₂ and c₁/c₂ tells you the number of solutions in a single line of work.
detailed.working_principle: If a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂, the lines intersect and there is a unique solution. If all three ratios are equal, the lines coincide. If the first two are equal but differ from the third, the lines are parallel.
applications: Intersecting lines: unique solution, consistent and independent.
Coincident lines: infinitely many solutions, consistent and dependent.

points: a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂ → infinitely many solutions (coincident lines).
a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂ → no solution (parallel lines).
Consistent means at least one solution exists.
Both equations must be in the form ax + by + c = 0 before comparing ratios.
mistakes: Comparing ratios before writing both equations in standard form.
Calling a dependent pair inconsistent; it is consistent with infinitely many solutions.
Mixing up the parallel and coincident conditions, which differ only in the third ratio.
topics.memory_hook: 'Two ratios differ → one point; all three equal → same line; only the last differs → never meet.'
topics.advanced: In matrix terms the pair has a unique solution exactly when the coefficient determinant a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ is non-zero. Cramer's rule then gives the solution directly, and the ratio conditions are that determinant in disguise.

topics.title: Algebraic Methods of Solution
topics.quick_summary: A pair of linear equations is solved algebraically by substitution, elimination or cross-multiplication, whichever suits the coefficients best.
topics.real_life: Splitting a bill where two items have unknown prices but two different totals are known is solved in seconds by elimination.

detailed.definition: In substitution, one variable is expressed in terms of the other and substituted. In elimination, the equations are added or subtracted after equalising one coefficient. Cross-multiplication uses a direct formula.
detailed.key_idea: Elimination is usually fastest when a coefficient is already equal or easily made so; substitution is easier when one variable has coefficient 1. Choosing well saves most of the arithmetic.
detailed.working_principle: Equations reducible to linear form, such as those involving 1/x and 1/y, are solved by substituting u = 1/x and v = 1/y, solving the linear pair, and converting back.
applications: Age problems, speed–distance–time problems, and work problems.
Boat and stream problems: upstream speed = b − s, downstream = b + s.
Fraction problems where numerator and denominator are both unknown.

points: Substitution: express one variable and substitute into the other equation.
Elimination: make one coefficient equal, then add or subtract.
Equations in 1/x and 1/y become linear after substituting u = 1/x, v = 1/y.
Always verify the answer in BOTH original equations.
mistakes: Forgetting to convert u and v back to x and y at the end.
Adding when the signs require subtraction during elimination.
Checking the solution in only one of the two equations.
topics.advanced: Cross-multiplication is Cramer's rule written out. For larger systems, Gaussian elimination generalises the elimination method and is what computers actually use to solve thousands of equations at once.

formulas.name: Cross-Multiplication Method
formulas.variables: a₁, b₁, c₁ and a₂, b₂, c₂ = coefficients of the two equations in the form ax + by + c = 0.
formulas.when_to_use: When both equations are already in standard form and the coefficients are awkward.
formulas.common_mistakes: Not writing both equations with all terms on the left before applying the formula.
formulas.shortcut: If a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ = 0, there is no unique solution — check the ratios instead.
